Ten bells. How many notes?

Selected: CsM I, Changsha Museum 1632.9. Shiguzhai, Hunan, China.

A: 280 Hz (C♯4, +17.5 cents). B: 269 Hz (C4, +48.1 cents). The selected B is -69.4 cents relative to A. Note names are modern reference labels, with A4 = 440 Hz. Moving this reference changes the labels, not the measured frequencies.

The app plays short sine tones at these frequencies. It does not reproduce the bells’ timbre or an ancient performance. The diagram locates strike areas schematically.

Ten bells from one find

Every frequency listed in the source table is retained. 87 plotted entries fall nearest to 10 modern keys in the octave C4–B4. This classification does not prove an ancient equal-tempered scale.

Read the evidence in context

The paper reports measurements made in August 2022 at 22 °C, using a wooden mallet and laptop recording. These are observations of surviving objects, not measurements taken in antiquity. Its authors argue that the bells could form a musical set; grouping, surviving condition and interpretation remain part of that argument.

The ten objects were found together in June 1993. The study dates their manufacture to the twelfth century BCE. Five other bells found in 1959 and two found in August 1993 make seventeen from the hill; this comparison includes only the ten with the June-find identities and full frequency lists.

Objects before categories

Names to carry with you

鐃 (náo): the mouth-up bell type studied here. 鐘 (zhōng): bell. 編鐘 (biānzhōng): an ordered set of bells. These are modern Mandarin readings, not reconstructed Bronze Age speech. See the app’s linked dictionaries and museum entry for the terms.
